newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Dhaka to open up power sector to private investors.
newsitem.headline: Dhaka to open up power sector to private investors.

text.p: Bangladesh said on Tuesday it would open its power sector to foreign and local investors and exempt them from tax and import duties.
A cabinet meeting on Monday approved a draft power policy aimed at attracting investment, Industry Ministry officials said.
Under the new policy, companies investing in the power industry would be given exemptions from value added tax, currently 15 percent, and duties on imported materials.
They would also be given a tax holiday, the officials said without giving details.
The decision comes as controversy grows over a proposal to import electricity to augment the country's lagging power supply.

"The new government is clearly in a dilemma on the issue because of growing opposition to import by its political rivals and public demand for uninterrupted supply of power to factories and homes," said one official who did not want to be named.
But the government was determined to go ahead with electricity imports, possibly from India, as well as setting up more generating plants locally to meet demand, the official said.
"We will go ahead with the idea of importing electricity from India or wherever it can be available at cheaper cost," Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina told a weekend meeting of her Awami League party.
"We need electricity because we want economic development. Nothing had been done in the past five years to improve the power sector," she said.

Opposition parties, including former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), say any deal to import power from India would be tantamount to surrendering the country's sovereignity to its big neighbour.

"A deep-rooted conspiracy is on against our sovereignty, independence and national existence," Khaleda told her followers on Thursday, adding the move to "import electricity from India is part of the conspiracy".
Bangladesh can produce 2,100 megawatts of electricity, leaving a shortfall of 200 megawatts, officials of the state-owned Power Development Board said.
They said the government had prepared a master plan for the power sector which foresaw the need for another 1,000 megawatts by 2000.

The government had recently floated an international tender for two 150 megawatt coal-fired power plants in northern Dinajpur, where Chinese companies were mining coal from a 300-million tonnes deposit, they said.

Board of Investment (BOI) officials said U.S. oil firm Unocal Corp and Canadian company Geopetrol International (1993) Ltd had put forward a joint proposal for setting up a 150 megawatt gas-fired power plant.

BOI executive chairman Tawfiq-e-Elahi Chowdhury said on Tuesday that the World Bank was expected to provide Bangladesh with $150 million to create a "private sector infrastructure fund" to encourage investment in the power sector.
"Hopefully the fund size will be about $300 million when the Asian Development Bank and other bilateral donors participate," Chowdhury told Reuters.
